headline: Diesel/middle distillate crack spreads in a relentless bull run toward $5.50/gallon, outperforming crude; Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries add a second supply disruption layer
reasoning: Weissman describes diesel crack spreads as the compelling story in the energy patch, with the move to $5.50/gallon per gallon being relentless and far stronger than moves in underlying crude oil. Supply constraints are driving middle distillates higher. The uptrend line has not been broken despite its acute angle, suggesting further potential retest of $5.50. An additional and often overlooked supply disruption is Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries. He also flags China's cancellation of refined product exports (both middle distillates and gasoline) as a new bearish supply factor for end consumers that lifted energy prices on the day.
quote: This move to the $5, 550 a gallon region has just been relentless, much stronger than the move in the underlying crude oil. Um, so the refined products, especially middle distillates like diesel, are really seeing this, um, this supply constraint just hitting them. And it looks like it's still quite bullish. That uptrend line, even though it's a pretty acute angle, has yet to be broken. So it's still a bull market. Still looks like we're going to potentially retest that 550 area... The other problem with middle distillates is that it continues to be, um, affected by these drone attacks of the Ukrainians against Russian refineries. So that's a whole other supply disruption piece that normally gets overlooked.
episode_title: Is Nasdaq strength masking broader weakness?

headline: Trump's proposed 90-day diesel export ban effectively shelved after administration pushback — risk of retaliation and domestic glut made it unworkable, but China refined product export cancellations are a new watch item
reasoning: Trump floated a 90-day ban on refined product exports expecting it to be popular, but feedback from his own administration caused him to backpedal once the risks of domestic oversupply, storage constraints and potential retaliatory cuts to US gasoline imports became apparent. The proposal is currently on the back burner. However, Weissman flagged same-day news of China cancelling refined product exports (middle distillates and gasoline), which caused energy prices to rise and warrants monitoring to see if it is a one-off or a trend.
quote: I think that he originally floated it and thought it would be popular, or thought that it would be well received, and then the feedback that he got from key members of his own administration made him kind of backpedal a little bit. Once he realized that you suddenly have this glut of diesel and potentially, you know, nowhere to store it, and the whole thing would backfire in terms of gasoline prices... what I did notice today was in the news feed, cancellations of exports of refined products, both, uh, middle distillates as well as gasoline, uh, from China. So if this is a one off, then maybe not such a big deal. But the markets did not like it today.

headline: Nasdaq challenging highs while Russell 2000 making new lows — divergence to resolve within 3-4 weeks, watching 28,000 as key Nasdaq level
reasoning: Weissman notes an interesting divergence: Nasdaq showing impressive strength and challenging highs while the Russell 2000 small/mid-cap benchmark is making new lows. He interprets this two ways — either institutional smart money is bullish and driving Nasdaq higher, or it reflects a lack of breadth which is bearish. He expects one of these two interpretations to become the dominant trend within 3-4 weeks. Key levels: a break of the 20-day low in Nasdaq (~28,000) would be bearish; a break of the 20-day high in Russell (about 50-75 points higher from current levels) would be bullish.
quote: It looks like Nasdaq is continuing to show really impressive strength, uh, challenging its highs and smaller cap Russell 2000 specifically is the benchmark that I use for small cap mid-cap. It looks like it's making new lows. So it's, um. It's an interesting divergence. You could look at it one of two ways. Either that the smart money, the institutional money is bullish and they're driving the Nasdaq higher, or that there's lack of breadth and therefore it's kind of bearish. Um, but I expect that one of these two will become the dominant trend over the next 3 to 4 weeks, we should get some resolution.

headline: Weekly downtrend intact, reflex rally failed at resistance; odds favour continuation lower with ~3,950 as the line in the sand, 4,675 needed to turn bullish
reasoning: Gold's weekly downtrend has remained intact. A Q3 reflex rally stalled at the downtrend line and reversed. We haven't hit the, um, the, uh, May lows yet, which I think is around 3950 area. So that would be kind of the line in the sand. If we can bounce there, then maybe it consolidates more and maybe even breaks the um, 46, 75 and then we go back up. But the odds do favor a continuation of the move to the downside, especially in this kind of yield increasing environment.

headline: Retail investors retreating to 5% Treasuries while institutional money piles into AI/Nasdaq dips — explains the breadth divergence
reasoning: Weissman attributes the Nasdaq/Russell divergence to a split in investor behaviour. Retail investors are looking at rising Treasury yields (~5%) and questioning why they should take equity risk when safe returns are available. Institutional money, by contrast, is focused on the AI narrative and treating pullbacks as buying opportunities, which has driven Nasdaq strength over approximately the past ten trading days.
quote: I think that smaller investors, retail investors are looking at yields and saying, why am I taking risk in this environment when I can get, you know, 5% on a treasury? Uh, and institutional money is looking at and saying, we've got these hot stocks, this AI story that won't quit. We've got a dip where we could buy a little bit lower. So let's pile on in. And I think that's what you've seen, especially over the past around ten, ten trading days.

headline: Bullish on diesel crack spread (heat crack) — a major breakout signals tightness and inflationary pressure in middle distillates, with round-number targets of 110 and possibly 125
reasoning: Weissman highlights the diesel/heating oil crack spread (heat crack) versus crude oil as showing a significant breakout that crude itself has not matched. This signals tightness in middle distillates — diesel, aviation fuel, farming and trucking fuel — and is an inflationary indicator. He sees this as a bull market in the short to intermediate term that has broken prior highs and has further to run. Key round-number targets are 110 and 125 on the crack spread, the latter being a level he expects major refineries would eagerly hedge.
quote: We see something really interesting in the price of diesel vis a vis the price of the raw material, crude oil. And we call this the crack spread, specifically the heat crack. It's it's how it's how much you get as a refiner. If you take raw crude oil and crack it into the middle distillates. And as you can see, unlike what we've seen in crude oil. We have a huge breakout in these middle distillates, and it shows you that things are tight and that it's inflationary. It's an inflationary sign. Who knows where the top of this thing is. It's obviously a bit frothy, but it looks like for the short to intermediate term this is a bull market that's broken the highs and probably has a ways to go... the market likes round numbers. So an obvious round number would be um 110 for that crack spread or even 125. That would be a really rich number that I'm sure major refineries would just jump all over and love to hedge at.

headline: S&P 500 looks toppy but no confirmed top yet — watching for break of 7300 as first warning, 6400 as deeper correction level while remaining in secular bull market
reasoning: Weissman notes the S&P 500 has defied gravity despite increasingly attractive risk-free yields, but he sees it as looking a little frothy. He is not yet calling a top — he needs to see a break of the week's lows for conviction. A break of 7300 would signal a minor correction, while a decline to 6400 in a higher-yields-for-longer environment would still be consistent with a longer-term bull market. He also acknowledges seasonal weakness in September–October as a potential headwind, offset by a possible Santa Claus rally.
quote: So so far it's resilient. It continues to kind of defy the law of gravity. You're getting more and more attractive yields on virtually risk free money. And yet it's holding up now. That's why I put a question mark. Is this a distribution top. Well obviously not yet because we haven't broken that support area. And even if we did break that support. But I'm really looking for. Would be a break of 7300 on the S&P. So that would be the first level of support. And that would just be a minor correction. I mean, I know it sounds like it's a long way from here, but it it wouldn't be a big deal. Certainly not a bear market. Um, if we do break that and we get this longer term higher yields for longer picture that I think is still developing, we could still have a significant correction all the way down to 6400 support and still be in a bull market longer term. So I do think it looks a little toppy I'd need for us to break the lows that we printed this week, uh, to get any real conviction that we put in a top and that those two levels are on the watch.

Um, so as you can see, there is a ways to go before we hit that long term support in 2006, it would be 104. Uh, and we're currently on the 107, close to 108 handle. So that would bring the yield another 100 basis points higher for the ten year treasuries, probably around five and a 4:45 .375 area. And, um, it does look like that's the trend. The trend is down in price, up in yield. So it's it's an interesting move. I'm not saying we're going to get there tomorrow, but potentially over the next 6 to 12 months that could be where we're headed.
